content.comment:
Thank you for your comment. We disagree, however, with your comments.

First of all, with a careful reading of our paper, it is easy to see that we do not have a single contribution limited to “convergence analysis” as [1]. In addition, even if it were limited to “convergence analysis” which [1] focuses on, our work significantly differs from, generalizes, and even improves upon Chen et al, 2019 in non-trivial ways. We emphasize that the proof leading to our Theorem 1 is **NOT** a mere copy-paste of Chen et al., 2019! We intentionally made our proofs follow the **same reasoning** (and made such correspondences) as [1] so that readers could better understand the differences and benefits of using block diagonal information.

Chen et al, 2019 focus on diagonal adaptation, while we consider the more general case of block-diagonal adaption. Our proof in Appendix F is for **general** full matrix adaptation (including diagonal cases as in Chen et al, and more general block diagonal case as in our paper). While our proof resembles that of Chen et al., 2019, it is significantly different: The analysis in Chen et al., 2019 heavily depends on the effective learning rate (i.e. for i-th coordinate, \alpha_{t,i} / \sqrt{\hat v_{t,i}}) for **all** coordinates. In contrast, the effective learning rate is absent in our block diagonal case: our proof in Appendix F depends on the matrix-vector product inequality involving matrix 2-norm (i.e. spectral norm, which means the maximum singular value of a matrix). Therefore, as a specific case of our Theorem 1, we can achieve strictly tighter bound in Term B for the diagonal case than Chen et al, 2019. In short, we generalize Theorem 1 in (Chen et al., 2019) to cover a broader class of adaptive methods, and can achieve strictly tighter bounds.
Moreover, we further investigate how the block size affects the convergence theoretically/empirically (see Section 3.1, especially **Corollary 1** and the discussions on the **convergence of EMA-based algorithms**).

We summarize the novelty of our paper as follows:
1)      We present a block diagonal adaptation method that can exploit the structural characteristics of deep learning architectures (Section 2).
2)      In terms of convergence, we verify that considering block diagonal adaptation can achieve faster convergence both in theory and empirical studies (Section 3.1).
3)      Also, we give intuitions that block diagonal adaptations have better generalization than the diagonal counterpart. As in convergence analysis, we demonstrate the effect of block sizes on generalization ability (Section 3.2).
4)      We propose extensions of our block diagonal adaptations such as spectrum-clipping/randomized scheme for better generalization/reducing computational cost (Section 4).
